title: Workload? More Like Working Loads!
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien maps a secondary teacher's Monday minute-by-minute to expose the gap between contracted hours (37.6/week) and actual demands -- a gap so large that only 5% of full-time teachers work within contracted hours, with 95% completing additional unpaid work. Using AITSL 2025 national workforce data, Brien contextualizes the systemic nature of teacher overwork: planning and preparation has decreased somewhat (possibly reflecting knowledge-rich curriculum adoption), while leaders spend roughly 50% of their time in meetings. Brien distinguishes between perception of workload -- which can be addressed culturally -- and structural realities, arguing that teachers often build resources individually when five colleagues teaching the same subject could share them, mistaking autonomy as resource creation rather than pedagogical flair. Drawing on Breakspear and Rosenbrock's Pruning Principle, he frames the fix as strategic subtraction: auditing every activity against time invested vs. value added, then eliminating what consumes without proportional benefit. Four practical levers are identified: streamlining communication channels, committing to high-quality shared curriculum resources, rethinking assessment practices to reduce correction load, and ensuring meetings have clear purpose and outcomes. The piece closes with the observation that professional learning -- the activity most likely to improve teaching quality -- is typically the first casualty of unsustainable workload.
points: AITSL data shows 95% of full-time teachers work beyond contracted hours, effectively reducing their hourly rate and destroying the life side of work-life balance.
Perception of workload -- not just actual workload -- drives burnout; many teachers invest in individual resource creation when shared resources would serve just as well with less effort.

Subject allocation disparities create huge workload inequities: a teacher with four different year-level subjects has radically more planning and assessment than one teaching the same subject at multiple levels.

The Pruning Principle framework (Breakspear and Rosenbrock) maps activities by time cost vs. value added, revealing that many high-time activities -- redundant emails, passive meetings -- are low-value.

Professional learning falls away first when workload becomes unsustainable, creating a downward spiral where the teachers most overloaded are least able to develop the practice that might ease the load.
quotes: Here we see that only 5% of full-time teachers are working for the amount of hours they are contractually paid for in their salary. Meaning that 95% of teachers are completing additional work out of hours, effectively decreasing their hourly rate and greatly reducing the life element of their work life balance.

I've gone on record before and stated that for many teachers it is not their actual workload which is burning them out, it is the perception of workload. That's not to say the workload of all teachers isn't high. However, as a profession we often aren't the best at putting measures in place to make our lives easier.

There is a perception that it is a teachers autonomy to plan and teach a class the way they feel comfortable, and to a degree that is true. As I've argued before though, autonomy doesn't come from creating the resources yourself, they come from how you inject your own personality and flair to bring them to life.

Meanwhile leaders are spending around 50% of their time in meetings which while important a lot of the time can mean they spend more time discussing rather than acting on school priorities and making the impact they ideally dreamed of when becoming a leader.

One question I always ask when planning a meeting is 'Could a staff member passively exist in this meeting and leave without needing to act on anything?'. If the answer is yes, then the meeting is unlikely to be effective and is likely to be perceived by the staff member as a waste of time and an increased burden on their workload.
